episodes.214990: A mesoscale convective system (MCS) that moved through Kentucky during the evening of August 11, 2026, kicked off a strong outflow boundary that moved south through Middle Tennessee which also helped to generate new thunderstorms. Strong winds associated with this outflow boundary caused a few downed trees and powerlines for locations east of Interstate 65.
episodes.215052: Isolated convection developed during peak diurnal heating over the Midlands and CSRA on 8/11 followed by a larger complex of storms that moved into the area later in the evening. Initial storms were generally along the Savannah River, leaving the central and northern Midlands environment generally untouched with moderate instability in place, despite weak wind shear. Storms moved out of the Upstate into the western Midlands and intensified with a significant wind signature observed on radar, a large area of 70+ knots radar estimated winds which resulted in numerous wind damage reports across Newberry County.
episodes.215062: From early morning through late evening on the 11th, a cold front interacting with a moist, highly unstable airmass sparked multiple rounds of severe thunderstorms across central Indiana. Upper-level disturbances supported recurring convective development, beginning with an initial morning wave in eastern counties followed by widespread squall lines and semi-discrete storms sweeping across western and central portions of the state during the afternoon and evening hours. This was the beginning of a multi-day severe and flash flood event with heavy rain and flash flooding towards the morning of the 12th.||Straight-line wind gusts ranging from 55 to 70 mph were the primary hazard, causing widespread tree damage, downed utility lines, and structural impacts across more than two dozen counties. Falling trees and large limbs blocked major roadways, damaged residential structures, and caused power outages throughout the region. Scattered severe cells also generated large hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter along with intense rainfall rates that led to localized street flooding before more intense flash flooding would begin later into the night.
episodes.215064: On the 12th, a quasi-stationary frontal boundary stalled across central Indiana, interacting with a deep plume of tropical moisture characterized by precipitable water values exceeding 2.0 inches. Anchored by a strong ridge of high pressure to the south, the lingering boundary provided sustained thermodynamic lift and convective instability over soil already saturated from severe weather on preceding days. Unidirectional atmospheric flow parallel to the surface front supported repeated cell training and high precipitation efficiency, driving prolonged periods of torrential rainfall and intermittent severe convective storms across central and southern Indiana.||Between 02:00 EST and 21:00 EST, successive convective cells traversed the region, producing extreme rainfall accumulations and localized severe weather. Peak 2-day precipitation totals reached 11.24 inches in Henry County, 10.69 inches in Randolph County, 10.27 inches in Delaware County, 8.79 inches in Madison County, 7.40 inches in Decatur County, and 6.48 inches in Jennings County. Straight-line convective wind gusts ranging from 58 mph to 62 mph uprooted trees and downed large limbs across Fountain, Hendricks, and Knox counties. At 14:03 EST, an EF-1 tornado touched down in Knox County near Bruceville, tracking 1.47 miles with a maximum path width of 150 yards and peak estimated wind speeds of 100 mph before lifting at 14:07 EST. The tornado snapped multiple groves of trees and damaged an outbuilding.||Excessive surface runoff produced widespread flash flooding that inundated infrastructure and primary transportation corridors. Floodwaters up to two feet deep submerged streets in Muncie, while standing water reached waist-deep levels in New Castle. Major roadway closures included US Highway 35, State Road 1, State Road 3, State Road 9, State Road 19, State Road 213, and State Road 244, with multiple vehicles stranded in floodwaters across Bartholomew, Johnson, and Tipton counties. Flash flooding washed out a culvert and destroyed a section of Riley Road in Henry County. Water intrusion into residential structures and commercial facilities resulted in basement flooding and forced localized evacuations at both a mobile home park and an apartment building in Henry County. This flash flooding would be followed by multiple days of historic river flooding across portions of central Indiana.
episodes.215105: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the Ohio Valley during a 36 hour period. Widespread wind damage occurred due to strong storms. Between 8 to 11 inches of rain fell across eastern Indiana, resulting in historic flooding in spots.
episodes.215106: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the Ohio Valley during a 36 hour period. Widespread wind damage occurred along with areas of flooding.
episodes.215107: Several rounds of thunderstorms moved through the Ohio Valley during a 36 hour period. Widespread wind damage occurred along with areas of flooding.
episodes.215142: On the 11-15th, several rounds of heavy to extreme rainfall within the upper White River watershed led to major flooding from Muncie to Indianapolis on both the White River and several tributaries.  One-day rainfall amounts:  through the early morning of the 12th were as great as 4-8 inches across all watershed areas east of Anderson; through the early morning of the 13th were up to 2-5 inches for most areas near and east of Anderson; with subsequent, less intense rains focused from the Tipton to Anderson areas;  leading to widespread 5-day totals through the 15th evening of 5-10 inches from northern Marion County to all watershed points north and east, including a large area of 9-13 inches from Anderson to the White River's easternmost headwaters in Randolph County.||Resultant major flooding impacted all points on the upper White River from Muncie down to Ravenswood, with the crest advancing from Muncie on the 13th midday to Ravenswood by the 15th late day;  including record crests at both Anderson (24.93 feet, surpassing 23.60 from 3/23/1904) and Noblesville (24.60 feet, surpassing 23.80 from 3/25/1913).  Significant flooding was ubiquitous over several White River tributaries, including crests in major flood on Fall Creek at Fortville (13th evening) and Cicero Creek at Arcadia (15th late day).||Flooding impacts ranged from evacuations in the Muncie and Indianapolis areas, to submerged roadways and highways in Delaware County and the Anderson and Edgewood parts of Madison County;  and inundated residential neighborhoods in Muncie, Yorktown, Riverwood, Noblesville, Federal Hill, low-lying portions of Fishers and Carmel, Ravenswood, Rocky Ripple and near Broad Ripple.  Ninety swift water rescues were needed in Hamilton County, and emergency floodgate operations were needed in northern Marion County. Approximately 2,500 structures were impacted across Delaware, Hamilton, Madison and Marion Counties.  Most notably the White River in Carmel flooded back up Blue Woods Creek, washing out the Hazel Dell Parkway bridge and overflowing as a waterfall into the Martin Marietta - North Indianapolis Mine.  Two fatalities occurred in Delaware County.||Outside of the broader river flooding, a culvert washout caused a fatality in Henry County after the flash flooding ended when a bicycler rode into the collapsed road and perished.
episodes.215246: A slow-moving storm system brought moderate to heavy rain to multiple locations over the course of two days. A recent dry spell and local drought impacts were able to absorb most of the rainfall. Aside from rainfall measurements, no additional impacts were reported.
episodes.215548: A cool cyclonic flow of unstable air moved across northern NY and VT during the afternoon and evening hours of August 12th. Scattered showers and thunderstorms occurred across the area with just a few storms in south-central VT producing isolated severe weather.
episodes.215953: Scattered thunderstorms developed north of a stationary front during the late evening hours on Tuesday (8/11) into the early morning hours on Wednesday (8/12).  The strongest storms produced large hail up to ping pong size and damaging winds across central Wisconsin.
episodes.216087: Severe thunderstorms tracked across northeast Colorado. Strong winds up to 81 mph were reported with the thunderstorms with several gusts of 55 to 75 mph being reported.
episodes.216143: During the mid-afternoon hours on the 12th, a cluster of severe thunderstorms materialized near the International Border, just south of El Centro with peak wind gusts likely exceeding 60 mph. Major damage to the electrical infrastructure was observed as over 150 power poles were compromised, resulting in over 5000 customers losing power at one point. There was also some other wind damage reports, including some downed trees and a large billboard toppled. Heavy rainfall from the thunderstorm cluster also resulted in scattered instances of flash flooding, with 1-2 falling within an hour according to doppler radar estimates. Strong outflow winds generated a large dust storm that surged northward through western Imperial County and into portions of Riverside County, including moving across the Salton Sea and Coachella Valley to the northwest. The overall environment that this thunderstorm cluster developed under was characterized by strong instability with MLCAPE values peaking at 2000 J/KG along with high Precipitable Water Values in excess of 1.7, supporting the potential for heavy rainfall. Alongside the favorable thermodynamic support, broad dynamic forcing was present thanks to a large-scale low pressure system positioned off the West Coast, which provided upper-level speed divergence to enhance the thunderstorm activity.
episodes.216238: A train of systems brought rounds of heavy downpours and strong to severe thunderstorms across the area while a frontal boundary wavered over northern Ohio and the Great Lakes region. A combination of very heavy rain and training storms led to flooding across portions of southeast Ohio and West Virginia.||Storms first originated in the Midwest during this time period, producing a long stretch of storm damage that encompassed the Ohio Valley into the Central Appalachians. Little to no time for atmospheric recovery was allotted before the next round of strong storms plagued the area. As a result, these episodic rounds of storms produced thousands of dollars in damage caused by powerful winds and heavy downpours. 72-hour rainfall amounts ranged from one to three inches in Gallia, Jackson, Lawrence, Meigs, and Vinton Counties and five to eight inches in Athens, Washington, Morgan, and Perry Counties. The heaviest amounts were observed in Perry and Morgan Counties, which set forth devastating flooding to the region. In addition to numerous flooded roads, water rescues, and rises on local creeks and streams, river gauges recorded flooding on Sunday Creek at Glouster, the Muskingum River at Beverly, and the Hocking River at Athens.
episodes.216303: Isolated to scattered strong to severe storms moved across I-80 in Wyoming producing strong wind gusts near Cheyenne. Severe storms across Nebraska produced hail, wind gusts, and a landspout. Severe Thunderstorm Watch 578 for western Nebraska.
episodes.216304: Isolated to scattered strong to severe storms moved across I-80 in Wyoming producing strong wind gusts near Cheyenne. Severe storms across Nebraska produced hail, wind gusts, and a landspout. Severe Thunderstorm Watch 578 for western Nebraska.
episodes.216404: On the 12th, sub-tropical moisture continued to increase over western NV, leading to widespread shower and thunderstorm coverage. The Sierra Front experienced areas of flash flooding during the afternoon, with Reno International Airport setting a new daily rainfall record of 0.60 inches.
episodes.216414: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the morning of August 12th producing scattered wind damage.
episodes.216415: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the late morning of August 12th producing isolated wind damage and one brief tornado.
episodes.216416: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the late morning of August 12th.
episodes.216521: A complex of thunderstorms across the lower Ohio valley tracked into the Piedmont, Sandhills, and Coastal Plain of central North Carolina during the afternoon and evening hours. Several damaging wind reports were observed, along with a few reports of quarter size hail.
episodes.216573: Multiple rounds of showers and thunderstorms produced a few wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.

This long duration of active weather was supported by a stationary front over the area, with heat, and exceptionally high levels of moisture.  Daily weak disturbances triggered storms.

This long duration of active weather was supported by a stationary front over the area, with heat, and exceptionally high levels of moisture.  Daily weak disturbances triggered storms.

This long duration of active weather was supported by a stationary front over the area, with heat, and exceptionally high levels of moisture.  Daily weak disturbances triggered storms.
episodes.216799: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.
episodes.217007: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.  Heavy rain resulted in localized flash flooding in Irwin county.
episodes.217011: Typical summer weather prevailed with scattered afternoon and evening storms, some of which were severe.
episodes.217210: Very heavy rainfall impacted parts of the region during the early morning hours of August 12. Several counties in eastern Indiana had the greatest impacts, with rainfall amounts of 4 to 8 inches. Some locations in northern and western Wayne County, received close to 10 inches of rain. This rainfall led to significant rises on the Whitewater River, which continued into August 14.
episodes.217219: On August 11, high pressure set up near the Four Corners, wrapping subtropical moisture around through Utah and into western Colorado. Most low-level moisture was depleted by mountain-driven storms in Utah, leaving mostly mid-to-high-level moisture to transit into western Colorado. While this diminished rain totals, this environment supported isolated thunderstorms capable of producing powerful downdrafts.
episodes.217220: On August 11, high pressure set up near the Four Corners, wrapping subtropical moisture around through Utah. Most low-level moisture was depleted by mountain-driven storms in central Utah, leaving mostly mid-to-high-level moisture to transit into eastern Utah. While this diminished rain totals, this environment supported isolated thunderstorms capable of producing powerful downdrafts.
episodes.217240: A disturbance moved through the region, bringing showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon and evening. Modest instability and weak wind shear supported scattered storms, with a few becoming strong to severe. Storms produced strong wind gusts and hail.
episodes.217242: A disturbance moved into the region from the Great Lakes during the late afternoon and evening, bringing scattered thunderstorms into the overnight hours. Despite limited surface instability, significant elevated instability supported development of scattered damaging hail and isolated strong wind gusts.
episodes.217243: A disturbance moved into the region from the Great Lakes during the late afternoon and evening, bringing scattered thunderstorms into the overnight hours. Despite limited surface instability, significant elevated instability supported stronger thunderstorms capable of producing hail and isolated damaging wind gusts.
episodes.217348: A cluster of thunderstorms pushed into northeast Nebraska during the early morning hours of August 12, 2026. Looking at the environment ahead of the storms, there was plenty of instability in place (4000+ J/kg of MUCAPE per SPS objective mesoanalysis) along with plenty of effective and deep-layer shear for the storms to remain organized. 0���3 km shear tapered off farther southeast, suggesting that as the storms moved into the area, they could become more outflow-dominant. However, guidance suggested 0���3 km shear would strengthen, or at least maintain, through the overnight hours. Factors working against the storms maintaining strength were a bit of dry air aloft and the primary forcing sliding by just to the north. Several pockets of wind gusts up to 70 mph were reported across northeast Nebraska. As the storms progressed to the southeast, they became less organized.
episodes.217388: Isolated thunderstorms in the morning produced hail of 1 to 2 inches in diameter to Allen County, Ohio.
episodes.217389: A line of thunderstorms exiting northeast Illinois was gradually weakening as it progressed through northwest Indiana. Isolated instances of damaging wind gusts were recorded and numerous reports of flooding were received. Antecedent conditions were very wet in Pulaski, Cass, and Grant counties (among others) with 2 to 5 inches of rain in the preceding 24 hours. Additional 24-hour rain totals by sunrise on the 12th were in the range of 3 to 5 inches.
episodes.217438: During the afternoon and evening hours of August 11th, multiple bowing segments developed and moved over central Kentucky and southern Indiana from northwest to southeast. The mid-afternoon wave was from a derecho that had originated in eastern Iowa during the early morning hours of August 11, moving through northern Illinois, Indiana, and Ohio before entering our forecast area. As the system was approaching north central Kentucky and far southeastern Indiana, it was moving into a very favorable atmospheric environment. Temperatures in the 90s and dew points in the low to mid 70s produced MLCAPE values around 3000-4000 J/kg. This wave was also at the nose of a 40-50 kt 500 mb jet that was producing 30-50 kt of deep layer shear. There was also ample atmospheric moisture in place, with PW values over 1.8. Considerable severe wind gusts and damage was experienced across north central Kentucky and southeastern Indiana, highlighted by an 81 mph wind gust at the Nicholas County Mesonet site. Another bowing segment would develop in eastern Illinois/western Indiana and travel southeast along the outflow boundary left by the initial system. Favorable environmental conditions allowed for scattered areas of wind damage to occur in southern Indiana and north central Kentucky. With the high moisture in place as well as additional development of showers and thunderstorms over south central Kentucky, some places that experienced repeated rounds of rainfall experienced some flash flooding. A round of repeated showers and storms occurred during the late overnight/early morning hours of the 12th. A few smaller bowing segments did develop that produced some brief damaging winds, however the persistent rainfall that lasted through most of the morning hours resulted in flash flooding for some places east of I-65. A line of showers and thunderstorms moved through southern Indiana and central Kentucky during the afternoon and early evening hours of the 12th, as well as a few isolated showers and storms over south central Kentucky. While environmental parameters were not as favorable given the repeated rounds of showers and storms, higher instability was in place over portions of central Kentucky that produced isolated areas of thunderstorm wind damage.
episodes.217482: Afternoon and evening thunderstorms caused areas of flash flooding across the region.
episodes.217518: A surface boundary spawned a cluster of storms in Wichita County. They moved east-southeast throughout the late afternoon evening hours. A 62 mph gust was measured two miles south of Leoti, KS.
episodes.217707: Common daytime heating and sea breeze influences resulted in scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms, as well as isolated strong to severe storms. Precipitable water values around 2.2+ inches and slow storm motion also resulted in multiple instances of very heavy rainfall and localized flooding.
episodes.217753: A warm, humid and unstable environment set the stage for scattered showers and thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon, some of which were proficient heavy rainmakers. An isolated instance of a road washout occurred as a result in Bradford County.
episodes.217857: A low pressure trough along the west coast and high pressure positioned to the east over eastern Texas allowed deep monsoonal moisture to continue to surge northward out of Arizona with precipitable water increasing to over an inch. Dynamic support increased a bit more to allow for more widespread thunderstorm activity, with thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall rates that resulted in debris flows across portions of western Colorado.
episodes.217928: During the morning hours of August 12th, a storm brought damaging wind gusts to portions of Schuyler County in NE Missouri, primarily in the Lancaster area and points east. Max wind gusts were likely up to 80 mph.
episodes.217935: A thunderstorm cluster tracked over southeast ND during the early morning hours and brought severe winds and wind damage to parts of rural Cass County ND.
episodes.217957: On August 12th, the region was under deep and unstable northwesterly flow and moist airmass. A passing upper shortwave triggered a convergent zone of numerous thunderstorms for locations from Waycross southeastward to the I-10 corridor. Stronger storms developed along this zone and along outflow boundary collisions. On August 13th, strong heating under ridging created enough surface based instability to pulse up storms inland that moved southeasterly into inland southeast Georgia in the afternoon. Slightly drier air increased the chance of downbursts (DCAPE 1000 J/kg) especially along boundary collisions.
episodes.218008: Weak forcing produced afternoon thunderstorms in a first wave, and then a pronounced vorticity maximum produced a round of extensive thunderstorms in the evening hours. The evening round was more widespread but both rounds produced damaging winds and flooding.
episodes.218019: A shortwave feature moved across the region late on August 10th into the early morning of August 11th following along a stationary boundary that has been situated along Lake Erie. A plume of 1500-2000 J/kg of MLCAPE developed across Northern and Central Ohio behind morning convection to go along with 40 knots of 0-6 km bulk shear and DCAPE of over 800.
episodes.218142: A subtropical high built across the central U.S. with weak troughing off the western U.S. coastline. This set the stage for robust moisture return into Utah, resulting in multiple instances of flash flooding across various locations in Utah. Across northern Utah, this system spawned a supercell which produced multiple instances of flash flooding across Tooele and Salt Lake counties, as well as numerous strong to significant severe wind gusts, large hail, and a tornado near the Skull Valley area in Tooele county.
episodes.218155: On August 12th, 2026, the Storm Prediction Center placed all of Western New York under a Marginal Risk (Level 1 of 5) for severe weather ahead of an approaching mid-level disturbance and weak surface trough. Area Forecast Discussions from NWS Buffalo highlighted modest daytime heating and boundary-layer moisture supporting scattered afternoon convective development, though mid-level lapse rates and wind shear remained unimpressive. Scattered thunderstorms developed along lake breezes and inland terrain boundaries during the afternoon and evening hours, producing localized robust cores. Across the NWS Buffalo CWA, the primary severe hazards were isolated strong-to-damaging downburst wind gusts and localized torrential downpours before activity dissipated with the loss of diurnal heating.
episodes.218187: Numerous severe thunderstorms developed in a conditional environment, with abundant low level moisture and instability but a strong cap in place. Supercells formed over southwest North Dakota after initiating on a weak confluence zone, and moved east into the south central. There were a variety of reports of severe hail extending from Slope County through Morton, Burleigh, and Stutsman. The most significant hail reports came from rural central Sioux County, where trained spotters reported hailstones up to 3.5 inches in diameter in the ditch, 30 minutes after the storm passed. There was also large hail up to the size of baseballs in the city of Lincoln in Burleigh County. There was only one severe thunderstorm wind gust reported from these storms, which was a measured gust of 68 mph near New Salem.
episodes.218228: Thunderstorms across San Bernardino County in southeastern California resulted in flash flooding and severe thunderstorm wind gusts.
episodes.218249: During the afternoon of August 12th, 2 rounds of discrete thunderstorms moved through Randolph County. The first dropped large hail and its outflow caused damage in Sparta. The second round produced wind damage in the rural southwestern portion of the county.
episodes.218255: Several severe thunderstorms affected western South Dakota on August 11th, 2026, including two particularly destructive and long-track supercells. One produced giant hail (up to 4 in diameter), and the other produced extreme winds (up to 111 MPH).||Giant Hail Producer (started in the Black Hills)|This long-track thunderstorm, and prolific and destructive hail producer, formed just after 1:00 PM MDT in the northern Black Hills. The storm initially sat over this area, shedding updrafts off its northern flank and struggling to move off the hills. It then matured into a supercell and started moving southeast, producing numerous reports of quarter (1.0��� diameter) to tennis ball size (2.50��� diameter) hail from near Nemo, to near Johnson Siding, to near Rockerville. Hail covered the ground and resulted in numerous broken windshields in the Rockerville area. The storm continued southeast experiencing several mergers, impacting the Hayward to Hermosa corridor with numerous reports of baseball (2.75��� diameter) and larger sized hail, with the largest received measurement coming in at 3.6��� diameter 2 miles south-southwest of Hermosa measured by a storm chaser. The hail fell for 10-15 minutes in some areas! Shattered home and vehicle windows, dented vehicles, broken downspouts and gutters, and a destroyed carport were reported in this corridor. In far southeastern Custer County, a reliable storm spotter reported a short-lived, long rope funnel from the storm. As the storm tracked through Oglala Lakota County, a swath of baseball (2.75��� diameter) to 4.00��� diameter hail was reported across the Oglala and Pine Ridge areas, causing widespread and catastrophic damage to homes, vehicles, and gardens/vegetation. Numerous home and vehicle windows were smashed out, and roofs were damaged. A school district in Oglala was forced to delay the start of their school year due to significant damage to 26 of their vehicles, including their entire fleet of 10 school buses. This storm exited South Dakota just before 7:00 PM MDT and would go on to produce more 3.5��� hail through north-central Nebraska.||Extreme Wind Producer (started in southeast Montana)|This destructive, long-track thunderstorm formed in far southeastern Montana, quickly becoming severe before moving into Harding County just after 4:00 PM MDT. The storm evolved into a high-impact, high-precipitation (HP) supercell for the first part of its lifespan tracking southeast across western South Dakota, producing damaging hail as large as baseballs (2.75��� diameter) and knocking down power poles between Camp Crook and Harding, and then intensifying and producing destructive winds ranging from 61 MPH to 111 MPH (13 miles northeast of Newell) across Butte County. Tree and structural damage was reported near Castle Rock. As the storm reached Meade County, the supercell structure deteriorated as more convection formed on its northeastern flank and the system started to elongate into more of a linear mode. It produced wind gusts to 79 MPH 3 miles northwest of Wasta, 84 MPH 2 miles east of Cottonwood, and 102 MPH 4 miles east of Cactus Flat as it reached the Interstate 90 corridor in Pennington and Jackson counties. Multiple vehicles including semi trailers were reported blown over along Interstate 90 near Wasta and Kadoka. Half-dollar size hail (1.25��� diameter) was also reported near Cedar Pass. Finally, the storm fully expanded/transitioned into a line as it continued to track southeast across Jackson, Mellette, Todd, and Tripp counties, producing widespread and significant wind damage. Wind gusts reached 83 MPH 4 miles west-northwest of Cedar Butte, 96 MPH 1 mile south of White River, 90 MPH 7 miles east-southeast of Rosebud, and 83 MPH in Wewela. Damage in Cedar Butte, White River, Mission, Rosebud, and Okreek included structural damage, outbuildings blown over, numerous trees snapped and uprooted, and windows blown out of homes and vehicles. The fairgrounds cook shack building in Rosebud collapsed, and the Tokala Inajinyo Youth Leadership Mentoring Program Resource Center 6 miles north-northeast of Rosebud was destroyed. Roofs were partially or completely blown off of multiple residences and businesses, and others had holes due to tree limb punctures. Per KELO-TV, severe wind damage rendered at least 53 homes uninhabitable across the Rosebud Reservation. North of Rosebud, an RV was blown over and rolled 50 feet, seriously injuring 1 person who was trapped inside and had to be cut out by firefighters. 78 power poles were also reported down or damaged across Mellette County. The storm exited into Nebraska by 1:00 AM CDT and continued to produce 60+ MPH wind gusts through northeast and eastern Nebraska.
episodes.218256: During the afternoon and early evening of August 12th, a cluster of thunderstorms pushed southeast through east-central and southeast Missouri. These remained severe over most of their lifespan and caused wind damage spanning from Warren County through St. Francois County.
episodes.218261: A supercell impacted portions of Fall River county with large hail and damaging winds.
episodes.218318: Weak forcing produced isolated afternoon thunderstorms in a first wave, and then a pronounced vorticity maximum produced a round of extensive thunderstorms in the evening hours. The evening round was more widespread but both rounds produced damaging winds and flooding.
episodes.218367: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms and some storm clusters developed over upstate  South Carolina throughout the afternoon and into the early evening. Multiple storms produced strong-to-severe damaging wind gusts along with isolated large hail.
episodes.218377: Isolated thunderstorms developed across upstate South Carolina during the late afternoon and evening. A couple of the storms produced brief damaging wind gusts in Greenville and Laurens Counties.

episodes.218572: Thunderstorms across Clark County in southern Nevada resulted in flash flooding and severe thunderstorm wind gusts.

There were numerous reports of widespread flooding across Wayne County. At least five to six feet of water covered much of Main Street in Cambridge City, inundating numerous businesses, homes, cars, school busses and more. As much as seven to eight feet of water inundated local neighborhoods. Multiple homes were later deemed unlivable and were demolished. Numerous trees were downed due to the amount of water. The flash flooding resulted in numerous high water and swift rescues. One rescue boat sunk due to rapid currents and was lost. ||In Hagerstown, several businesses were inundated with two to three feet of water, mud, and debris. Water inundated the high school football stadium, ticket booth, and bleachers. The wastewater treatment plant power building was also inundated with around two feet of water and a neighboring residence was inundated with five feet of water. ||Other cities like Richmond, Williamsburg, and Centerville also experienced widespread flash flooding, with water inundating yards, basements, and streets.
